name: Desia
confidence_why: Mahapatra (1985), the only work that describes Desia stress at all, calls it both predictable and phonemic, gives minimal pairs, and marks it on the first, second or final syllable in different examples, while Datta (2002) and the other works read say nothing about stress, so no placement or type can be stated.

All monosyllabic utterances carry the highest degree of stress. In words of more than three syllables there is always secondary stress on some subsequent syllables and usually it falls on that syllable which is farthest from the primarily stressed syllable. ... new_statements.quote: 3.4. Stress—/'/. Stress has phonemic value on a very limited number of words in Desia as it is a predictable phoneme in this dialect. All monosyllabic utterances carry the highest degree of stress. In words of more than three syllables there is always secondary stress on some subsequent syllables and usually it falls on that syllable which is farthest from the primarily stressed syllable. e.g. /'pas/ cave, /kə'rat bar/ to dig with spade, /gu'e'ta/ tick, /se'tuwali/ centiped, /a'dar/ dark. Stress is more distinctive in utterances with consonant/sonant/clusters in the first or second syllable. e.g. /'tanḍ/ mouth, /as'ti/ property, /kanḍe'k/ a bit. [p. 39:] Final vowel—Final /ə/ is seldom retained on account of stress on initial syllable. jərə—jər (fever), kakərə—kakər (cold)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source calls stress predictable (phonemic only in a handful of words) but never states the primary-stress position outright. The one explicit positional remark says final /ə/ is lost 'on account of stress on initial syllable', and the noun members of the minimal pairs carry initial stress ('pala 'seedling', 'duar 'door', 'kəla 'soot', 'sapa 'clean') while the verb-form members carry final/non-initial stress (pala' 'go away', du'ar 'you carry', kə'la 'he did', sapa' 'whole lot'). The examples in 3.4 itself, read with the stress mark preceding the stressed syllable, show second-syllable stress (kə'rat, se'tuwali, a'dar, as'ti), which conflicts with the initial-stress remark unless the mark is read as following the stressed syllable ('indicated by /'/ on the side', p. 11). Net: leaning toward default initial word stress with grammatically conditioned non-initial stress in verb forms, but the description is internally ambiguous.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'In words of more than three syllables there is always secondary stress on some subsequent syllables and usually it falls on that syllable which is farthest from the primarily stressed syllable' (p. 29).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress is contrastive in 'a very limited number of words'; the contrast pairs (p. 15) oppose nouns with initial stress to verb forms with final stress; stress said to be 'more distinctive' when there is a consonant cluster in the first or second syllable; monosyllables carry the highest degree of stress. Phonetic (non-phonemic) vowel length falls 'in the penultimate position of a closed syllable and in the final position of a consonant cluster' (p. 38).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for 'utterances' and 'words' in citation-style examples (grammar based on the author's Koraput fieldwork); no phrase-level or instrumental data. The stress mark's placement convention is not fully consistent between p. 15 and p. 29, so the position reading should be reviewed against the page images before cataloguing.
new_statements.identity_note: desi1235 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping node: Glottolog states Desiya [dso] and Adivasi Oriya [ort] 'simply divide the speakers of the same language along a state border' and points to adiv1239 (Kotia-Adivasi Oriya-Desiya). The source quoted (Mahapatra 1985) describes the Desia spoken in Koraput district, Odisha, i.e. exactly the [dso] side; the Andhra Pradesh side (Kotia/Adiwasi Oriya) was described separately by Gustafsson (SIL, 1974/1989), not examined here.
